note: What happened on each night, from dated public sources. Times are local. Where sources differ, the entry says so. Countersign's side of the page comes from evals/results/nights.json, measured on the deployed stack.

nights.title: Hawaii, January 13, 2018
nights.failure: A drill sent as real, by one person, and 38 minutes to correct it.

events.text: A no-notice drill begins at a shift change. The recording says "exercise" and also "this is not a drill".
One warning officer, believing it real, picks the live template and confirms. The alert goes to every phone in the state. No second person had to sign.
The officer's own phone sounds. It is the watch center's first sign the alert went out.
The agency's director tells the governor the alert is false.
A cancellation stops rebroadcasts. It sends nothing to the phones.
The agency posts "no missile threat" on Twitter. Phones still show the alert.
Staff choose a message code for the correction. There is no correction template.
A supervisor starts writing the correction.
The correction reaches phones, 38 minutes after the false alert.

nights.contested: Hawaii's own report puts the send at 8:06; the FCC puts it at 8:07. The FCC's preliminary report has the Facebook post at 8:20, its final report at 8:23.
nights.reach: It reached 1.4 million residents and about 200,000 visitors.

nights.title: Los Angeles County, January 9 and 10, 2025
nights.failure: One fire zone's evacuation warning sent to the whole county, then sent again before dawn.

events.text: Staff begin drafting an evacuation warning for Calabasas, Agoura Hills and West Hills, near the Kenneth Fire.
It goes to the whole county. The map area was saved for every channel except the phone channel, the county code filled itself in, and the software gave no warning.
Cancelled, 2 minutes 47 seconds after it went out.
A correction goes out, about 20 minutes after the false alert.
The same wrong alert reaches phones again before dawn. The county acknowledges it nearly three hours later.

nights.contested: The repeat alert is reported as around 4 AM (CBS Los Angeles) and 4:24 AM (LAist); no official time was found. The congressional report gives 3:56 PM for the first alert and about 20 minutes to the correction; USA Today reported the correction at 4:19 PM.

nights.title: Kerr County, Texas, July 4, 2025
nights.failure: The weather service warned all night. The county sent no phone alert of its own.

events.text: The weather service issues a flood watch for Kerr County.
First flash flood warning for Hunt, Ingram and Kerrville. The weather service's own alert reaches phones.
Water enters a riverside cabin at Camp Mystic.
About now the Hunt gauge nears 10 feet and the camp starts moving campers from riverside cabins.
The warning is extended to 7 AM. Four to eight inches of rain have fallen.
Flash flood emergency for Hunt: the weather service's highest level.
The Hunt volunteer fire department asks for a CodeRED message.
The county's first CodeRED goes out, for the Hunt area only. CodeRED reaches only people who signed up for it.
The Hunt gauge crests at 37.52 feet, the highest on record.
About now, by their own account, the county judge and the emergency coordinator wake up.
Flash flood emergency from Hunt through Kerrville and Center Point.
Neither the county nor the city sends a phone alert through FEMA's system. 117 people died in Kerr County, 37 of them children.

nights.contested: The county's first CodeRED is 5:01 in the sheriff's account and 5:02 in city records. The flash flood emergency is 4:03 in the product itself; some accounts give 4:04 or 4:23, when it was posted online. The camp's evacuation is about 3 AM in the legislative report; early family accounts said 2 to 2:30.
nights.reach: About 52,600 people live in Kerr County.
